title: RunGood Poker Series Hits Houston
deck: The Golden Expedition at Champions Club Houston features $510K in guarantees and 11 ring events.
author: Shomari Williams
caption: RunGood Golden Expedition at Champions Club Houston
body:
For the first time ever, the RunGood Poker Series is coming to Houston. The RGPS Golden Expedition runs October 12–18, exclusively at Champions Club (6440 W Sam Houston Pkwy S, Houston), with $510K in published guarantees and 11 championship rings up for grabs. The headliner is a $600 Main Event with a $250,000 guarantee.

Champions Club is offering a tournament room rate starting at $79 a night for players who want to stay and play. Club membership is required to play, and the structure sheet lists the fee portion of each buy-in as a "facility access fee."

The Main Event is the best-priced event on the schedule, with a 16.7% fee on a $600 buy-in, a 60,000 stack, and 30-minute levels. The $400 events (Monster Stack, PowerStack, Last Chance) run 17.5%, and the $300 events run 20%. If you're picking one event this week, the Main gives you the most structure for your money.

Graded from the Champions Club structure sheets with the TSR Score calculator:
• Monster Stack Opener ($400, 50,000 stack, 30-minute levels): TSR 69.8 (B−). 17.5% fee, with playable depth through level 19.
• RunGood Main Event ($600, 60,000 stack, 30-minute levels): TSR 66.0 (B−). 16.7% fee. Same letter as the opener, slightly lower score, and the best fee of the three.
• PokerNews PowerStack ($400, 40,000 stack, 30-minute levels): TSR 46.6 (D+). 17.5% fee. Same buy-in as the Monster Stack, but the 40,000 stack and faster blind climb cut depth to level 15.

Fee percentage still favors the Main, but structure favors the Monster Stack. The PowerStack is the softest of the three on skill depth.

Sources: RunGood event page, Champions Club structure sheets (PDF), PokerNews preview, and the Champions Club Texas email announcement (Oct 10, 2026).

title: Jesse J Wins the Trailblazer Kick Off
deck: Stop 2 opens with a 347-entry field and a $114,510 prize pool at TCH Dallas.
author: Shomari Williams
caption: Final Kick Off payout board on the TCH Dallas stream
body:
Jesse J is the Trailblazer Stop 2 Kick Off champion. The $400 #1 Kick Off ($100K GTD) at TCH Dallas drew 347 entries for a $114,510 prize pool (TCH live report). That beat the guarantee easily, and 44 places were paid.

Final results (as shown on TCH's live stream):
1. Jesse J: $20,980
2. Natalia: $20,250
3. BJ: $10,950
4. Chase Bricker: $7,090

It came down to Jesse J and Natalia. At Hand 44, with blinds at 50,000/100,000/100,000, the stream's chip-count graphic had Jesse J on 5,870,000 and Natalia on 4,810,000. Jesse J and Natalia struck a heads-up deal, and Jesse J took the title.

Fourth place went to Chase Bricker. He's the Dallas-area player who beat Jason Christopher heads-up at Wynn Las Vegas in December 2024 to win the $1 million first prize in the ClubWPT Gold $5M Invitational Freeroll (PokerNews, WPT). No trophy this time, but a deep run on home felt.

The Kick Off was just the opener. Trailblazer Stop 2's $800 Main Event ($1,000,000 GTD) starts its first flight at TCH Dallas on Monday, Oct 12 at 5 PM, with flights through Oct 17 and the final table Oct 19 (official schedule). I'll be on it.

— Sham

title: They Sent Undercover Agents to Play $1/$2… and THIS Is What They Came Up With?
deck: After a nine-month undercover investigation, six covert visits, bank records, the IRS, and a 22-page affidavit at The Lodge in Round Rock, here is how the case stacks up against the 2019 Houston raids.
author: Shomari Williams
body:
Originally posted March 17, 2026.

When I first read the March 17 update on the TABC search-warrant affidavit regarding The Lodge, I almost didn't want to give my opinion right away — I needed a moment to calm down first, because something about this looked really, really fishy.

Once I sat down with the details, one question stood out: They sent undercover agents to play $1/$2… and THIS is what they came up with?

By now you've seen the headlines. The Lodge Card Club in Round Rock is dark. Assets frozen. Hundreds of employees displaced. And after a nine-month undercover investigation, six covert visits, bank records, the IRS, and a 22-page affidavit, the biggest case they could build rests largely on large deposits from a cash business and one agent who got lucky enough to play without a membership.

"Call the floor because we need a new setup."

Now let me be clear: nobody has been charged with anything. No arrests have been made. And in America, you are innocent until proven guilty. But when you stack this situation up against the 2019 Houston raids on Post Oak Poker Club and Prime Social — where nine people were actually arrested, $10 million was frozen, and all of those charges were eventually dropped — you start to wonder exactly what standard is being applied here.

One thing is certain: competition in Texas poker is fierce, on the felt AND off the felt.

The Lodge San Antonio? Still open. Same company. Same ownership. Make that make sense.

Texas poker has always survived on skill, resilience, and community. The rooms are still running across DFW and the games are good. But stories like this remind us that the legal landscape in this state remains gray by design.

We're watching this one closely. The Sham Report is where we cover Texas poker the way it deserves to be covered — real analysis, real talk, no fluff. Stay locked in.

— Sham

title: No Affidavit. A Business Shut Down. Assets Frozen. Is This How Due Process Works?
deck: Doug Polk broke his silence on The Lodge Card Club raid with a detail that should concern every Texas poker player: the search-warrant affidavit still hadn't been given to The Lodge or made public.
author: Shomari Williams
body:
Originally posted March 16, 2026.

No affidavit. A business shut down. Assets frozen. Hundreds of employees displaced. Is this how due process works?

Doug Polk finally broke his silence on The Lodge Card Club raid, and what he revealed should concern every Texas poker player.

In his written statement, Polk emphasized that he did not participate in, and had no knowledge of, any money laundering in the operation of The Lodge, while pledging that members with chip balances and tournament payouts would be made whole in coordination with his attorneys.

The most important line in his entire statement? "That affidavit has not been given to the Lodge or made public."

The people whose business was shut down didn't even know the specific allegations against them at that point. No arrests. No charges. Just a closed door and hundreds of employees out of work.

A search warrant is not a conviction. But right now it's being treated like one.

I would love to hear your thoughts and opinions on this ongoing issue.

— Sham

title: When You Speak With Honesty and Compassion, People Feel It: A Nod From Andrew Neeme
deck: In the middle of the hardest week in The Lodge's history, poker vlogging pioneer and Lodge co-owner Andrew Neeme took a moment to acknowledge our coverage.
author: Shomari Williams
body:
Originally posted March 16, 2026.

I want to share a small but meaningful moment with you all.

When I wrote my post about The Lodge situation, I made a conscious decision to lead with fairness and compassion rather than speculation and judgment. I didn't know if anyone beyond the DFW poker community would even see it.

Well, Andrew Neeme reacted to the post.

For those who don't know who Andrew Neeme is, he is widely considered the godfather of poker vlogging. He is the pioneer who showed the world that the poker lifestyle was worth capturing and sharing. He inspired an entire generation of content creators — myself included — to pick up a camera and tell their stories. Without Andrew Neeme, the poker content community as we know it looks completely different.

Andrew is also one of the principal partners of The Lodge Card Club. So when I say this situation hits close to home for him, I mean that in every sense of the word. This is his business, his passion, and his livelihood.

The fact that he took a moment in the middle of what has to be an incredibly stressful and difficult time to acknowledge this post means more to me than I can fully express. I want him and his wife Busi to know that the poker community sees everything they have built and we are rooting for them.

Speak with honesty. Lead with compassion. People will always feel when something is genuine.

Andrew, we're with you. I hope The Lodge finds its way back to the felt very soon.

— Sham

title: Shuffle 214 $100K Series Recap: Five Bullets, One Min-Cash, and the Truth About Tournament Variance
deck: Five $150 entries into Shuffle 214's $100K GTD series came back with one $250 min-cash for a -$500 net — and a reminder of why cash games pay the bills.
author: Shomari Williams
body:
Originally posted March 13–14, 2026.

Walked into Shuffle 214 on Friday night with $100,000 on the line — Flight 1H at 6 PM on Friday, March 13, followed by Saturday's Flight 1I at 11 AM and Flight 1J at 6 PM. Call a $150 buy-in a donation if you want; going in, I called it an investment.

Here's the final ledger:
• Event: Shuffle 214 $100K GTD Series
• Bullets fired: 5 entries at $150 each
• Total invested: $750
• Return: 1 min-cash for $250
• Net result: -$500

That's poker. No shame in it.

But here's how I look at it: I'm not a tournament-to-tournament grinder. For players who go hard every single week chasing big fields, tournament variance can be absolutely brutal on your bankroll and your mindset. I've seen it. I respect the dedication, but that's not my game plan.

My next move is back to cash games. A solid week of grinding $1/$2, $1/$3, and $2/$5 and that $500 is very easily recovered, with profit on top. That's how you keep poker manageable and repeatable.

And honestly? When I wrapped the tournament at 6 PM, the night was still young.

— Sham

title: Operational Gaps vs. Criminal Intent: The Community Adds Real AML & KYC Context to the Lodge Story
deck: Readers Jon Waters and Abram Evan Fontana pointed to a crucial distinction in the Lodge investigation: how Texas's unregulated gray area leaves rooms exposed on Anti-Money Laundering and Know Your Customer compliance.
author: Shomari Williams
body:
Originally posted March 14, 2026.

I want to take a moment to thank everyone who has been engaging in the comments around The Lodge situation. The poker community knows how to band together, and you're not just reacting emotionally — you're bringing real knowledge and perspective to a complicated story.

Two comments in particular stood out to me, and I want to highlight them because they add important context that may reframe how we should be looking at this.

Jon Waters made a really interesting point: Resorts World in Las Vegas faced a similar money-laundering investigation and they were never shut down. His take is that this doesn't necessarily mean Doug Polk or anyone on his team was directly involved in laundering money. It's more likely that a few dishonest players found small loopholes in the operation that didn't have strong enough barriers in place to stop them. That's a very important distinction between criminal intent and operational vulnerability.

Abram Evan Fontana then took it a step further by bringing up AML — Anti-Money Laundering laws — and Know Your Customer (KYC) compliance protocols. Here's what that means for those who may be unfamiliar: licensed casinos in regulated states are required to have entire compliance departments dedicated to monitoring suspicious financial activity. They are heavily regulated and legally forced to build those protections. The Lodge, operating in Texas's legal gray area, never had that same regulatory structure forcing them to build that infrastructure to the same standard.

So what both of these gentlemen are essentially saying is that it's very possible The Lodge became vulnerable not because of deliberate criminal activity by ownership, but because operating in an unregulated environment left gaps that someone took advantage of. And in the eyes of the IRS and TABC's Financial Crimes Unit, a gap is a gap regardless of intent.

This doesn't excuse anything if laws were broken. But it does add important nuance to a story that has a lot of people speculating.

Keep the dialogue coming. This is what the poker community is about. And yes, I read all the comments.

— Sham

title: My Two Cents on The Lodge Situation: Why the Gray Area Is the Real Weapon Against Texas Poker
deck: Doug Polk became the most visible, politically organized voice pushing for legal clarity in Texas poker — and that context matters when looking at what's happening in Round Rock.
author: Shomari Williams
body:
Originally posted March 13, 2026.

Let me be clear upfront: I don't know Doug Polk personally. Never met the man. So I'm reserving full judgment on the current investigation until the facts come out. No arrests. No charges. Just an ongoing investigation at this point.

But here's what I DO know.

When Doug Polk came to Texas, he didn't just come to run a poker room. He came with ambition and he put his money where his mouth was. He and his partners, Andrew Neeme and Brad Owen, acquired majority ownership of The Lodge Card Club in Round Rock in 2022, building it into the largest poker room in Texas. Then in 2024 they purchased Rounders Card Club in San Antonio, rebranding it as The Lodge Card Club San Antonio and expanding their footprint even further.

But beyond the business moves, Doug became something Texas poker didn't really have before: a legitimate, organized political voice.

He helped launch Texans for Texas Hold'em, a lobbying group created to protect the social poker club model and push for legal clarity in Texas gambling law. He worked directly with state legislators on bills like HB 2345 to formally legalize membership poker clubs. He appeared before city councils, including in Farmers Branch right here in DFW, fighting for zoning rights so new rooms could open. He used his massive YouTube and social media platform to educate players, mobilize the community, and keep pressure on lawmakers. That's not nothing. That's real advocacy work.

Now here's my theory — and I want to stress this is just a theory.

Texas poker has been under attack long before Doug Polk ever showed up. I've been playing in this state since 2014, and the legal gray area has always been a weapon used against this community. The uncertainty isn't an accident; there are powerful interests who benefit from keeping Texas poker in limbo because it means they can shut you down at any moment.

Doug Polk became the most visible, most vocal, most politically organized threat to that gray area. And now his room is the one being investigated by a financial crimes unit with the IRS involved.

Do I think Doug, Brad Owen, and Andrew Neeme are suddenly the Texas Poker Mafia? Naw. I don't buy that at all. Is it possible there are financial issues within the operation that need to be addressed? Sure — and if laws were broken, then handle it accordingly. We need poker rooms that set the right example.

But let's not lose sight of the bigger picture. Texas poker is under attack. It was under attack before Doug got here, and it'll be under attack after this situation resolves. The people who want this industry gone are still out there and they are still organized.

I hope for the sake of the employees, the players, and the future of Texas poker that The Lodge finds its way back to the felt in Austin. And to Doug, Brad, Andrew, and the entire Lodge team, I wish you all the best of luck, because honestly this fight is far from over.

If you own a poker room in Texas right now, just know: you could be next. This isn't paranoia — it's the reality of operating in a state where the law still hasn't given this industry the protection it deserves. Stay sharp. Stay clean. Be safe out there.

This is Sham, aka ShamGod Poker, signing off. I'm proud to be part of this Texas poker community, and I'm looking forward to staying in this fight with all of you.

— Sham

Doug Polk became the most visible, most vocal, most politically organized threat to that gray area. And now his room is the one being investigated by a financial crimes unit with the IRS involved.
Do I think Doug, Brad Owen and Andrew Neeme are suddenly the Texas Poker Mafia? Naw. I don't buy that at all. Is it possible there are financial issues within the operation that need to be addressed? Sure, and if laws were broken, then handle it accordingly. We need poker rooms that set the right example.

But let's not lose sight of the bigger picture. Texas poker is under attack. It was under attack before Doug got here and it'll be under attack after this situation resolves. The people who want this industry gone are still out there and they are still organized.

I hope for the sake of the employees, the players, and the future of Texas poker that The Lodge finds its way back to the felt in Austin. And to Doug, Brad, Andrew and the entire Lodge team, I wish you all the best of luck, because honestly this fight is far from over.
If you own a poker room in Texas right now, just know, you could be next. This isn't paranoia, it's the reality of operating in a state where the law still hasn't given this industry the protection it deserves. Stay sharp. Stay clean. Be safe out there.

This is Sham, aka ShamGod Poker,  signing off. I'm proud to be part of this Texas poker community and I'm looking forward to staying in this fight with all of you.

title: Lodge Card Club Update: TABC Financial Crimes and the IRS Were Behind the Raid
deck: TABC confirmed its Financial Crimes Unit, the Williamson County Sheriff's Office, and the IRS executed the search warrant at The Lodge over suspected money laundering and illegal gambling — not a liquor-license check.
author: Shomari Williams
body:
Originally posted March 12, 2026.

Thanks to the DFW poker community for keeping me plugged in as this develops.

We now have answers on why TABC raided The Lodge Card Club in Round Rock on Tuesday, March 10 — and it's bigger than anyone initially assumed.

According to a statement from TABC Director of Communications Chris Porter to PokerNews (https://www.pokernews.com/news/2026/03/lodge-card-club-money-laundering-charges-50804.htm), the agency's Financial Crimes Unit, along with its Special Investigations Unit and Operations Bureau, executed a search and seizure warrant as part of an ongoing investigation into suspected money laundering and illegal gambling.

Early speculation centered around liquor licensing issues or underage drinking, which makes sense given TABC's name. Those assumptions appear to have been incorrect.

Approximately 20 TABC agents were involved in the operation, along with officers from the Williamson County Sheriff's Office and the IRS. The IRS being involved is significant — this is a federal-level matter.

No arrests have been made and no charges have been filed against the business at this time. The investigation remains ongoing, and The Lodge remains closed with no reopening timetable announced.

We will continue to follow this story closely.

— Sham

title: Lodge Raid Coverage: Tom Dwan Enters the Chat
deck: A day after the raid, Tom Dwan jumped into a tense X exchange with Doug Polk — and the story started splitting into two different versions.
author: Shomari Williams
body:
Originally posted March 12, 2026.

The Lodge Card Club in Round Rock remains closed following Tuesday's search warrant executed by state police and TABC. The Lodge's official statement says their attorneys are still working to understand the reasons behind the search, meaning even they don't fully know why yet.

Now poker legend Tom Dwan has inserted himself into the conversation, with his own separate allegations.

Dwan is claiming he warned Doug Polk years ago about a game integrity vulnerability at The Lodge and that Doug chose not to address it. Dwan has been careful to say he does not believe the TABC raid is connected to that issue, but the timing has the poker world asking questions.

Worth noting, Dwan has also acknowledged personal friction with Doug, so we're not dealing with a completely neutral party here.

Bottom line: Two separate stories colliding at the worst possible time for The Lodge. The TABC situation is still unresolved. And now there are integrity questions being raised publicly by one of the most respected names in the game.

We're watching this closely. I'd love to see your comments.

— Sham

title: The Lodge Raid: First Reaction (March 11, 2026)
deck: My first reaction when news broke that TABC raided The Lodge in Round Rock — before any official statement or confirmed details.
author: Shomari Williams
body:
Originally posted March 11, 2026.

By now most of y'all have probably seen the news. TABC and state police rolled up on The Lodge in Round Rock Tuesday morning around 11 a.m. Biggest poker room in Texas, co-owned by Doug Polk, Brad Owen, and Andrew Neeme. Players were told to take their chips home and come back when they reopen. Staff told tournament players they'd be refunded entries. The WPT Wildcard event that was supposed to happen this weekend has been postponed.

No official statement from the owners yet. No confirmed citation details that I've seen.

Now here's the part that's been on my mind since I heard about this. The Lodge is an 18+ room. That's something a lot of people didn't realize, including me honestly. When you mix 18- and 19-year-olds in the building with alcohol service, TABC showing up starts to make a lot of sense. Whether it was underage drinking, a license issue, how alcohol was being distributed, whether it was free or sold, all of that matters legally and none of it has been confirmed yet.

Texas poker rooms already operate in a gray area. Add alcohol into the equation with players who are legal to gamble but not legal to drink and that's a real compliance problem for any club.

If anybody has actual confirmed info on what the citation was for, drop it in the comments. This situation has implications for every poker room in Texas and we need to be paying attention.

— Sham
